BrandGuard Preflight
Product plan | Inkloom AI problem statement | 25 October 2026
Team: Somnath (Team Lead, MERN Full Stack Developer) | Falguni Sharma (MERN Full Stack Developer) | Om
Apar (AI/ML Specialist)
Preflight checks content before it goes out. Every claim in a draft is compared with the
company's own approved guidelines, facts and past content. When we can prove a problem,
we show the proof and suggest a fix that keeps what the writer meant. When we can't prove it
either way, a person decides.
1. Problem definition and evidence
Most growing companies have brand guidelines, but in

practice nobody checks content against them. Writing
now comes from employees, agencies and AI tools, and mistakes like a wrong claim, an old price, off-tone
wording or an off-brand image often reach the public before anyone spots them. The surveys below come from
vendors and trade press, so read them as a rough guide, but they all tell the same story:
85% of organisations have brand guidelines but only about 30% enforce them consistently; 77% regularly
deal with off-brand content (Marq).
47.1% of marketers meet AI inaccuracies several times a week and 36.5% say incorrect AI content

has
already gone public (NP Digital, 565 US marketers).
50% of consumers prefer brands that avoid GenAI in consumer-facing content; Gartner advises labelling AI
use (1,539 US consumers).
Most tools look at how a piece of writing sounds. We also check what it says: is each claim true, is it current,
and does it match what the brand has already published?

1.2 Root causes behind the failures
Guidelines are written for people, not machines. A rule like "keep a friendly but professional tone" can't be
checked the same way twice, so enforcement depends on who happens to review.
Facts have no owner and no expiry date. Prices, customer counts and policies change, but old copies stay
in decks, posts and web

pages and nobody is told.
Feedback comes late and without a reason. Problems show up after publishing or after several review
rounds, so people start working around review.
1.3 Design tensions we must resolve
Tension
Our position
Speed vs control
Automate only what can be proven exactly; route everything unproven to a person with
the evidence attached
Catching more vs being
trusted

Local-first design, redaction preview before any external call, and a mode with the model
switched

off
Strict rules vs creative
freedom
Suggestions are opt-in and overrides need a reason; repeated overrides signal an unclear
rule to fix, not a person to blame
1.4 A typical failure, step by step
Step
What happens today
Where it goes wrong
1
The returns policy changes from 14 days to 30 days.
The policy page is updated.
Nobody is told that older posts, decks and FAQs now
contradict it.
2
A new agency writer drafts a promotional post from an
old brief that says "14 days".
The guidelines don't mention return periods, and the
writer has no way to look up the current fact.
3
An AI tool rewrites

the post and adds "the best returns
in India".
The new claim has no evidence behind it, and the tool
sounds confident.
4
The brand manager skims the post, likes the tone and
approves it.
Checking facts and claims was never part of the
review, and she is reviewing 40 other items.
5
The post goes live. A customer quotes it at the support
desk.
The error is found by a customer, after the damage is
done.
Preflight steps in at step 2 and 3: it shows the writer the current policy next to the draft, and it asks legal about
the superlative before the post goes anywhere near the brand manager.
1.5 What

a good solution has to do
Catch problems before publication, not after.
Base every judgement on the organisation's own approved material, so results can be checked.
Explain each issue and offer a fix that keeps the writer's purpose, so people learn and don't work around it.
Hand anything uncertain or risky to the right person, with the evidence ready.
Keep confidential material inside the organisation and say clearly when AI or an outside service is used.

A creator's journey
Priya, a marketer, uploads a draft and fills in a short intent form: purpose, audience and two must-say
points.
Preflight returns four findings in under a minute. Two are verified, one is a contradiction with the

returns
policy, one is a superlative with no evidence.
She accepts the fix for the policy error and edits the suggested rewrite of the superlative.
The "best returns in India" line has no evidence, so it is routed to the product and legal reviewers as a
question. She keeps working on the rest.
The legal reviewer rules that the claim can't be used. The ruling is saved so the next writer who tries the
same claim is told straight away.
Her manager approves the new version, a Brand Passport is saved, and Priya publishes.

What makes us different, in one line: instead of judging how content sounds, Preflight checks what it says
against the company's own approved facts and its own published history, and every human ruling becomes
knowledge it can reuse. We haven't seen these ideas emphasised together:
Findings that can't exist without a cited source passage: no source, no violation.
Contradiction checks against the brand's own past

content.
Claim Shelf-Life: facts have owners and expiry dates, and the owner is warned before one lapses.
Intent Lock: every fix comes with a note on what it keeps and what it drops.
Guideline Debugger and Rule Simulator: guidelines get tested and improved like any other asset.
Brand Passport: a tamper-evident record for each approved asset, including whether AI was used.
